# How to Use Gemini to Generate Rubrics in Google Classroom

> **In short:** Google Classroom now lets teachers draft rubrics with Gemini, Google's AI assistant, right in the assignment page. Describe the assignment, generate a draft, edit it, and attach it — so the blank-page work that used to eat your Sunday night can be done in minutes.

It's 9 pm on a Sunday, and you're planning tomorrow's essay assignment. You still need to write a rubric from scratch. You open a blank Google Doc, stare at it for ten minutes, and start typing "criteria" and "points" like it's 2010. There's a faster way now.

Google has added a feature that lets you draft a rubric inside Google Classroom using Gemini (Google's AI assistant — think of it as a writing partner that lives inside Google's apps). You describe your assignment, and Gemini suggests a starting rubric you can edit and use. Here's how to try it.

## What you'll need first

Before you start, make sure you have:

- A **Google Workspace for Education** account with access to Google Classroom (this feature is part of Google's education tools, so a personal Gmail account won't have it)
- An **assignment you're about to create** in Classroom — have a rough description ready
- About **five minutes**

If your school already uses Google Classroom, you most likely have everything you need. If you're a tutor or homeschool parent, look into Google Workspace for Education — there's a free tier that includes Classroom, though some newer AI features may be limited to paid school accounts.

## Step 1 — Open the assignment creation page

In Google Classroom, click the **Classwork** tab at the top, then choose your class. Click **Create** (the plus sign), and select **Assignment** from the dropdown menu.

You'll land on the assignment creation page, where you fill in the basics: title, instructions, due date, points. Don't worry about the rubric yet — that's next.

**You'll know it worked when:** you see the title field, the instructions field, and an attachments area. That's the assignment creation page.

## Step 2 — Find the Rubrics section

Scroll down the assignment creation page until you see a section labeled **Rubrics**. This is where your grading criteria live. If you've never made a rubric for this class, the section will be empty. If you have, you'll see your previous rubrics listed there.

In that Rubrics section, look for an option to create a new rubric. The exact wording varies as Google updates the interface, but it's usually a **Create rubric** button or a plus icon next to the section title.

**You'll know it worked when:** you can see the Rubrics section and have clicked into the new-rubric area.

## Step 3 — Choose the Gemini option

When you start creating a new rubric, Classroom will offer a few options. One of them is to draft the rubric with help from Gemini, Google's AI. The button might be labeled **Generate with Gemini**, **Draft with AI**, or something similar — Google's interface updates often, so look for any option that mentions Gemini or AI.

Click that option. Classroom will pull in the context from your assignment — the title and instructions you already typed — and use that as the basis for the rubric draft.

💬 **Example prompts you can use to refine the draft:**

- *"Add a row for creativity and originality."*
- *"Make the language level appropriate for 7th graders."*
- *"Reduce the total points to 20 and rebalance the rows."*

**You'll know it worked when:** Gemini shows you a draft rubric with rows (criteria), columns (performance levels), and point values.

## Step 4 — Review and edit the rubric

This is the step most teachers skip — and the one that matters most. AI-generated rubrics are a starting point, not a finished product. Read every row, and ask yourself:

- Does each criterion actually measure something my students did?
- Is the language at the right level for my students?
- Are the point values fair?
- Did I miss any criteria that matter for this assignment?

Click into any cell to edit the wording or adjust the points. You can add rows, delete rows, and rename performance levels (for example, changing "Excellent" to "Exceeds Expectations" to match your school's terminology).

**You'll know it worked when:** the rubric reflects your teaching values and the specific skills you actually want to assess — not generic-sounding AI filler.

## Step 5 — Attach the rubric and share it with students

Once the rubric looks right, save it. Classroom will attach it to your assignment automatically. Now, decide whether students can see it.

By default, rubrics are usually teacher-only. To share with students, look for a **toggle or checkbox labeled something like "Share with students"** — you can usually find it in the **rubric sidebar on the right side of the screen**, or under the **three-dot menu (⋮)** at the top of the rubric panel. Switch it on, then save again.

A good practice: **share the rubric with students before the due date** so they know how they'll be graded. Rubrics shared in advance usually lead to better work and fewer disputes.

**You'll know it worked when:** the rubric appears under the assignment and is ready to use for grading once students submit.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- **Generating a rubric before writing the assignment description.** Gemini uses your assignment context, so a vague description produces a vague rubric. Write the instructions first, then generate.
- **Publishing the AI draft without editing it.** The first draft is rarely the final one. Always read it through and adjust for your students, subject, and standards.
- **Using criteria that are too vague to measure.** "Good effort" and "nice presentation" sound fine but don't help you grade fairly. Push the AI toward specific, observable criteria: *"Uses at least three pieces of textual evidence per paragraph"* beats *"Shows understanding."*
- **Forgetting to share the rubric with students.** If students can't see how they'll be graded, the rubric only helps you — not them. Sharing it turns the rubric into a learning tool.

## What this means for you

- **If you're a classroom teacher:** This feature can save you real time once you build a workflow around it. Start with one assignment this week — generate, edit, share — and see how it feels before rolling it out to everything you teach.
- **If you're a homeschool parent or tutor:** You can use the same workflow to create rubrics for writing assignments, science projects, or presentations. It works just as well for one student as for thirty.
- **If you use simpler assessments:** The feature shines most for assignments with multiple grading criteria (essays, projects, presentations). For a quick quiz, a basic rubric is still faster to write by hand.

## Wrap-up

AI-generated rubrics aren't about replacing your judgment as a teacher — they're about getting to the thinking part faster. Let Gemini do the blank-page work, and you do the expertise work: tuning the criteria, matching them to your standards, and adjusting for the students actually sitting in front of you.

Here's your next step: open Google Classroom right now, pick one assignment you haven't created a rubric for yet, and run through the five steps above. Five minutes from now you'll have a working draft you can tweak — and your next Sunday night just got a little less stressful.
